lead: A level gives readings, not ground heights. The field book turns each staff reading into a reduced level (RL) by one fixed rule: a reading is subtracted from the height of the instrument line. Two layouts do this: height of collimation keeps one instrument height until the level moves; rise and fall compares consecutive readings. The fixed columns and two arithmetic checks let you find a mistake before you leave the site, when re-reading is easy and cheap.
prereq: You need: the definitions of datum, benchmark and reduced level from Chapter 3.1, the temporary adjustment of a level from Chapter 3.2, and the backsight–foresight pattern from Chapter 3.3.

blocks.text: The field book is written before any arithmetic. Each row is one staff position: a benchmark (BM), an intermediate point, or a change point where the instrument moves. Columns are station, backsight (BS), intermediate sight (IS), foresight (FS), rise, fall and reduced level (RL). A reading is the height of the line of sight above the staff zero, not the ground height.
In the height of collimation method, also called the collimation method, one instrument height is computed for each set-up:

blocks.where: HI is height of collimation in metres, RL is reduced level of the point carrying the backsight, and BS is that backsight reading in metres.

blocks.text: Each later reading from the same set-up is subtracted from this HI: RL = HI − IS or RL = HI − FS. The foresight is the last reading before the instrument moves, so that station becomes a change point. On the next set-up a new backsight is taken on that change point and a fresh HI is formed. The old HI is not carried across.

items: Write the benchmark and its known RL; take the BS and compute HI.
For each IS, subtract the reading from HI and write the RL.
For the FS, subtract from HI; mark that station as a change point.
Move the instrument, take a new BS on the change point and compute a new HI.

blocks.text: Rise and fall compares consecutive readings. If the next reading is smaller, the ground rose: the line of sight sits lower above the ground. If the next reading is larger, the ground fell. Store the difference as a positive number in the correct column.
rise = previous − next (when previous > next); fall = next − previous (when next > previous)
blocks.where: previous and next are consecutive staff readings in metres; each difference is written as a positive number in the rise or fall column.

blocks.text: Then RL = previous RL + rise, or RL = previous RL − fall. Work down the page. A change point simply has a new BS and a new comparison continues.

This method shows the exact line where a wrong entry was made. For a profile or cross-section, that is useful because each rise or fall is also the ground slope between two points. A fall of 0.30 m is written as 0.30, not −0.30; the heading carries the sign.

Two checks run down the columns. For either method, ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL. Intermediate sights appear in neither ΣBS nor ΣFS. They are not part of the instrument-height change, and in the rise-and-fall sum each intermediate reading cancels as a next reading and later as a previous reading.
ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL
blocks.where: ΣBS and ΣFS are column sums in metres; ΣRise and ΣFall are column sums in metres; first and last RL are the first and last reduced levels in metres.

blocks.text: Use the height of collimation layout for speed: fewer lines of arithmetic are written for many intermediate sights. Its check does not test the intermediate-sight subtraction, so an arithmetic slip there can pass the check. Use rise and fall for profile and cross-section work and for locating mistakes, because each line shows the comparison that produced the reduced level.

items: Change point: a station read as an FS, then as a new BS.
HI method: quicker on long runs of IS; the check leaves IS arithmetic untested.
Rise and fall: slower, but the error line is visible.
Both methods: run the checks on site, before the instrument is packed.

examples.question: The following readings were taken with a level: 2.50 m on a benchmark of RL 50.00 m (BS), 1.80 m on A (IS), and 2.10 m on B (FS). Book and reduce the levels by the height of collimation method and by the rise and fall method. Apply the arithmetic checks.
steps: Write the readings in order: BM 2.50 m (BS), A 1.80 m (IS), B 2.10 m (FS). The benchmark RL is 50.00 m.
Checks: ΣBS − ΣFS = 2.50 − 2.10 = 0.40 m; ΣRise − ΣFall = 0.70 − 0.30 = 0.40 m; last RL − first RL = 50.40 − 50.00 = 0.40 m. The IS 1.80 m is in neither ΣBS nor ΣFS.
examples.answer: Height of collimation 52.50 m; RL of A = 50.70 m; RL of B = 50.40 m; all checks equal 0.40 m.
examples.check:
bs = 2.50
is_ = 1.80
fs = 2.10
bm = 50.00
hi = bm + bs
rl_a = hi - is_
rl_b = hi - fs
diff = bs - fs
print(hi)
print(rl_a)
print(rl_b)
print(diff)

traps: Writing a rise where the next reading is larger. A bigger reading means lower ground: a fall is next − previous, not previous − next.
Putting intermediate sights into ΣBS − ΣFS. The check then fails on a correct book; IS values belong in neither column sum.
Carrying the old HI across a change point. Every change point gets a new BS and a new HI.
Writing a fall as a negative rise. Keep both rise and fall columns positive; the column heading supplies the direction.
Checking only one pair of quantities. The three values ΣBS − ΣFS, ΣRise − ΣFall and last RL − first RL must all agree.

quiz.q: Name the two common methods of booking and reducing levels.
quiz.a: Height of collimation, also called the collimation method, and the rise and fall method.

quiz.q: Write the three-part arithmetic check used with a levelling field book.
quiz.a: ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL.

quiz.q: Why does a larger staff reading mean lower ground?
quiz.a: The staff is read against the horizontal line of sight. A larger reading means more staff is exposed between that line and the ground, so the ground is lower.

quiz.q: Why are intermediate sights left out of ΣBS − ΣFS?
quiz.a: They are taken without moving the instrument, so they do not change the instrument height. In the rise-and-fall sum each intermediate reading cancels as a later previous reading.

quiz.q: A benchmark has RL 25.00 m. Readings are BS 1.60 m, IS 2.35 m and FS 1.20 m. Reduce by the height of collimation method and apply the check.
Readings on a benchmark of RL 100.00 m are 1.40 m (BS), 1.05 m (IS), 1.75 m (IS) and 1.20 m (FS). Reduce by rise and fall and check.
quiz.a: RLs are 100.00, 100.35, 99.65 and 100.20 m. Rises are 0.35 m and 0.55 m; fall is 0.70 m. ΣRise − ΣFall = 0.20 m; ΣBS − ΣFS = 0.20 m; last RL − first RL = 0.20 m.

quiz.q: A book gives ΣBS − ΣFS = 0.30 m, ΣRise − ΣFall = 0.30 m, and last RL − first RL = 0.25 m. What does this tell you?
quiz.a: The arithmetic check fails. At least one reduced level, one column sum or one change-point entry is wrong. Re-add the columns and re-check each change point before leaving the site.

quiz.q: Why is rise and fall preferred for a road profile even though the HI method is quicker?
quiz.a: Each line shows the comparison and the exact station where an error enters. The rises and falls also read directly as ground slope between consecutive points, which is what a profile shows.

beyond: Not for the exam. Digital levels and total stations log readings and compute reduced levels inside the instrument, but the same column checks remain in the firmware. Modern field software stores a raw reading beside a reduced level, so a wrong instrument height can be corrected later without rebooking the whole page. Search for digital level field book, level book reduction software, or automatic level data logger.
